pedagogy.summary: Children come to see that area and perimeter are INDEPENDENT: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. The work is systematic — fix one quantity (say area 24 cm²) and generate rectangles that differ in perimeter (a long thin 1×24 has a large perimeter; a squarer 4×6 a smaller one). The misconception to dislodge is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). It is best taught by having children build many shapes with a fixed area or perimeter and tabulate the other, so the variation is SEEN, not asserted — and by probing reasoning, since a correct answer can still come from the faulty intuition.
bestPractices: Fix one quantity and vary the shape systematically (all rectangles of area 24; all shapes of perimeter 20), tabulating the other so children see it change.
Confront the 'Same A – Same B' intuition head-on with counterexamples (a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16).
Use squared paper and tiles so children construct and count rather than rely on a remembered rule.
Probe reasoning beyond correct answers — a right answer can come from the intuitive rule, so always ask 'why' (Tsamir & Mandel).
Link to practical intuition: a long thin field and a square field can hold the same crop area but need very different lengths of fence.
keyRepresentations: Squared paper / tile arrangements at fixed area
Table of dimensions versus perimeter (or perimeter versus area)
Long-thin-versus-square rectangle pair with equal area
Fence/string model for perimeter around a fixed area
commonMisconceptions: 'Same A – Same B': believes shapes with equal area must have equal perimeter (or that changing sides by equal-and-opposite amounts leaves both unchanged).
Conflates area and perimeter, so cannot hold one fixed while varying the other.
Thinks making a shape 'bigger' must increase area and perimeter together.

learn.summary: Children learn that knowing one of area or perimeter does NOT determine the other: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. (They are not completely unrelated, though: for example, a fixed perimeter limits how large the area can be.) The core work is systematic — fix one quantity (e.g. area 24 cm²) and generate shapes that differ in the other, tabulating so the variation is SEEN, not asserted. The target misconception is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). Because a correct answer can come from the faulty intuition, always probe the reasoning.

activities.title: Lock the area, watch the perimeter change
feedback: If the perimeter is reported as unchanged, re-count the edge units of the 1×24 and compare with the 4×6 — the long thin shape needs far more edge.
Prompt: 'The surface still covers 24 squares. Why does the distance around keep growing?'
A 'fence/string' overlay makes it concrete: the same crop area (24 squares) needs a longer and longer fence as the rectangle gets thinner.
activities.rationale: Fixing one quantity and tabulating the other lets children watch independence happen rather than be told it; squared paper supports constructing and counting over recalling a rule. The fence/string overlay and auto-filling table are optional supports that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'recognise that shapes with the same areas can have different perimeters and vice versa'.

Year 6 Mastery PD develops the generalisations 'Shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas' and 'Shapes can have the same area but different perimeters' through matchstick/squared-paper tasks (e.g. four shapes of area 16 units² with perimeters 34, 20, 16 and 26 units), reminding children that perimeter is measured in length units and area in square units.
learnerActions: Start from a 4×6 rectangle on squared paper (or a drag-to-reshape grid) that reads 'Area 24 cm², Perimeter 20 cm'.
Reshape it to 3×8, 2×12, then 1×24, keeping the area pinned at 24 cm² each time.
After each shape, count the squares to confirm the area is still 24, then count the edge units to find the new perimeter (20, 22, 28, 50 cm).
Record each rectangle's dimensions and perimeter in a table so the growing perimeter is visible alongside the unchanged area.
Say aloud what stays the same and what changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping area fixed while reshaping shows the perimeter climbing even though the covered surface is unchanged, so same area does NOT force same perimeter.

activities.title: Lock the perimeter, watch the area change
feedback: If a child expects the areas to match, compare the 5×5 (area 25) with the 1×9 (area 9) — same perimeter 20 cm, very different area.
Prompt: 'Same length of fence every time — why does the amount of ground inside change?'
activities.rationale: Showing the 'vice versa' direction (fixed perimeter, varying area) prevents a one-sided understanding and reinforces independence both ways, matching the statutory 'and vice versa'.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'recognise that shapes with the same areas can have different perimeters and vice versa'.

Year 6 Mastery PD develops the generalisations 'Shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas' and 'Shapes can have the same area but different perimeters' through matchstick/squared-paper tasks (e.g. four shapes of area 16 units² with perimeters 34, 20, 16 and 26 units), reminding children that perimeter is measured in length units and area in square units.
learnerActions: Fix a perimeter (e.g. 20 cm) and build several rectangles that all have that perimeter: 1×9, 2×8, 3×7, 4×6, 5×5.
For each, count the squares to find the area (9, 16, 21, 24, 25 cm²) and record it in a table.
Note which shape gives the largest area and which the smallest for the same perimeter.
activities.intendedInsight: With perimeter held constant, the area varies — so same perimeter does NOT force same area either; in both directions, fixing one quantity does not fix the other (although the fixed perimeter does cap the area: here the 5×5 square gives the most).

activities.title: The string test (predict, then check)
feedback: If the prediction was 'same area so same distance around', treat that stated reason as the thing to revisit: count the edges of each before and after testing with the string.
If a child argues 3×4→2×6 'takes off one and adds on, so it evens out', compute both perimeters explicitly (14 vs 16) — the changes do NOT cancel; the perimeter changed even though the area did not.
If area and perimeter are reported as a single number, re-separate the meanings: area is the squares covered, perimeter is the distance around.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain task with an actual counterexample surfaces the reasoning that produced the answer, so a lucky correct area is not mistaken for understanding. Asking for a fresh example checks that the child can generalise rather than treat it as a one-off.
sourceClaims: Many learners hold the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same perimeter → same area; same area → same perimeter). Counterexample: a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16. Learners believe increasing one pair of sides and decreasing the other by the same amount leaves area and perimeter unchanged ('is like you did nothing'). Correct answers found via an intuitive rule do not reflect understanding (Tsamir & Mandel 2000), so teachers must probe further.
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 rectangle and a 2×6 rectangle on squared paper; confirm both have area 12 cm² by counting squares.
PREDICT whether one loop of string will go exactly around both, and say WHY before testing.
Lay the string around each and measure: the 3×4 needs 14 cm, the 2×6 needs 16 cm.
Draw a THIRD rectangle with area 12 but yet another perimeter, and find the largest perimeter you can make for area 12 (with whole-number sides, the thinnest 1×12 gives 26 cm).
activities.intendedInsight: Both rectangles cover the same area (12 cm²) but their perimeters differ (14 cm and 16 cm) — a direct counterexample to 'Same A – Same B'.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic
feedback: If the child only states the answer, push for the justification tied to a specific pair (e.g. 3×4 vs 2×6, or 1×9 vs 5×5).

If the child agrees 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter', give a direct counterexample: a 5×5 square (area 25 cm², perimeter 20 cm) has a LARGER area than a 1×24 rectangle (area 24 cm², perimeter 50 cm) yet a much SMALLER perimeter — so a bigger area does not force a bigger perimeter.
activities.rationale: Requiring the child to construct an argument and generate counterexamples targets the reasoning the misconception rule hides. This dialogue form builds explanation but, on its own, does not provide the visual variation the construction tasks do, so pair it with them.
sourceClaims: Many learners hold the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same perimeter → same area; same area → same perimeter). Counterexample: a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16. Learners believe increasing one pair of sides and decreasing the other by the same amount leaves area and perimeter unchanged ('is like you did nothing'). Correct answers found via an intuitive rule do not reflect understanding (Tsamir & Mandel 2000), so teachers must probe further.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists 'same area must mean same perimeter' and 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter'.
Build or draw counterexamples and use them to explain, in your own words, why the character is wrong.
Answer the follow-up: 'If two shapes have the same perimeter, must they have the same area? Show me two that don't.'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reason — that area and perimeter vary separately — consolidates understanding beyond producing a correct answer.

constraints: Perimeter is measured in length units (cm) and area in square units (cm²); keep these distinct when recording and comparing.
A correct answer can still come from the faulty 'Same A – Same B' intuition, so always ask 'why' and require a justification or a fresh example.

Multiple-choice or sequencing items can diagnose the misconception via distractors but do not by themselves produce the 'aha'; pair any recognition task with construction (drawing/building and counting).
A single static equal-area pair with revealed perimeters gives one counterexample but does not let the child vary the shape; use it as a starter, not the whole lesson.
Use squared paper or tiles so children construct and count rather than rely on a remembered rule.

To refute 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter', use a pair where the larger-area shape has the smaller perimeter (e.g. 5×5 area 25, P 20 vs 1×24 area 24, P 50); an equal-area pair alone does not address a 'bigger area' claim directly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

All quantitative examples were re-checked: area-24 rectangles 4×6 (P=20), 3×8 (P=22), 2×12 (P=28), 1×24 (P=50) are correct; perimeter-20 rectangles 1×9 (A=9), 2×8 (A=16), 3×7 (A=21), 4×6 (A=24), 5×5 (A=25) are correct; the 3×4 (A=12, P=14) and 2×6 (A=12, P=16) counterexample is correct; the 5×5 (A=25, P=20) vs 1×24 (A=24, P=50) counterexample for 'bigger area' is correct.

The original 'possible: 3D adds nothing' claim was dropped as an unsupported universal; the topic is planar so 2D construction is the natural medium, but this is a scope note, not a proven claim about 3D's inability to teach.

The non-preferred conversation and static-image approaches are retained as 'Convince the sceptic' and a starter scaffold respectively, with their limitations noted in constraints rather than as universal laws.

The 'largest perimeter for area 12' answer (1×12 → 26 cm) holds only for whole-number-sided rectangles as used in these Year 6 tasks; for arbitrary shapes perimeter is unbounded, so frame the question within the rectangle context.

assess.poeTask: Show the two rectangles (3×4 and 2×6) and a length of string. Ask the child to PREDICT whether the same loop of string will go exactly around both — given they cover the same area — and to say WHY before testing. Then lay the string around each: the 3×4 needs 14 cm, the 2×6 needs 16 cm. The reason given before observing (typically 'same area so same distance around') is the diagnostic part; the string makes the independence undeniable.
probeDeeper: You said the areas are equal — count the squares to check. Now count the edge lengths. Are the perimeters equal?
Can you draw a THIRD rectangle with area 12 but a different perimeter again? What is the largest perimeter you can make?
If two shapes have the same perimeter, must they have the same area? Show me two that don't.
A friend says 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter.' Is that always true?
assess.correctAnswer: Both have area 12 cm² (same area), but their perimeters are 14 cm and 16 cm (different) — so the same area can have different perimeters; area and perimeter are independent.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Same A – Same B': because the areas are equal, concludes the perimeters must be equal too.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the edge units of each on squared paper; tabulate several equal-area rectangles and their differing perimeters so the independence is seen, then re-ask.
errorPatterns.distractor: Same area and same perimeter — if the area is the same, the distance around must be the same too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the perimeters are the same 'because the areas are the same'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It balances out': reasons that shrinking one side and growing another leaves both area and perimeter unchanged.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute both quantities for each rectangle explicitly and show the perimeter changed even though the area did not; stress the changes do not cancel.
errorPatterns.distractor: The perimeter stays the same because one side got shorter while the other got longer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Argues going from 3×4 to 2×6 'takes off one and adds on, so it evens out' and both stay equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates area and perimeter, computing one and reporting it as both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-separate the meanings — area as covered squares, perimeter as distance around — before comparing the two rectangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single number for 'area and perimeter', or measures the distance around when asked about area.

responseLevels.gap: Asserts that equal area forces equal perimeter (Same A – Same B) with no checking.
responseLevels.full: Shows the areas equal and perimeters different, explains that area and perimeter vary independently, and generates further shapes with fixed area and changing perimeter (or vice versa).
responseLevels.partial: Correctly finds both quantities for the given pair but treats it as a one-off, or reaches the right answer via 'it balances out' without seeing area and perimeter as independent; cannot generate a new example.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rectangles: one is 3 cm by 4 cm, the other 2 cm by 6 cm. Do they have the same area? Do they have the same perimeter? Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'Same A – Same B' and a child who understands independence give OPPOSITE answers to 'same perimeter?'. The reason they state — areas equal therefore perimeters equal, versus area and perimeter vary separately — exposes which, so a lucky correct area is not mistaken for understanding.
